variants.title: Unbounded in-memory queue
variants.context: Producers keep appending jobs in RAM while workers are stuck, and the process OOMs.
variants.constraint: Work arrives faster than it completes.
variants.question: What should producers see?
variants.expectedPattern: A bounded queue that blocks, drops, or returns 429 when full instead of growing forever.

variants.title: Accept then collapse
variants.context: The API returns 200 for every upload even though transcode workers are 6 hours behind.
variants.question: What signal is missing?
variants.expectedPattern: Apply backpressure at ingest (slow down or reject) when downstream capacity is exceeded.

variants.title: TCP buffer hides overload
variants.context: A client keeps sending because the kernel buffer is large, then the server dies at once.
variants.question: Where should pressure propagate?
variants.expectedPattern: Stop reading or send a full/busy signal so senders slow down before collapse.
wrongChoices: Larger kernel buffers as the only defense

variants.title: Stream without demand
variants.context: A reactive pipeline requests unbounded data from Kafka and blows the heap.
variants.question: What is the streaming rule?
variants.expectedPattern: Request only as many records as you can process (consumer lag + pause, or reactive demand).
wrongChoices: Buffer the topic in the app

variants.title: Autoscaling too late
variants.context: CPU hits 100% and the queue is 2 million deep before scale-out starts.
variants.question: How does backpressure help in the meantime?
variants.expectedPattern: Reject or delay new work at the edge while scaling, instead of accepting an unbounded backlog.
wrongChoices: Keep accepting until disk is full

variants.title: Downstream 429 ignored
variants.context: A payment API returns 429 and the worker retries immediately in a tight loop.
variants.constraint: The vendor asked you to slow down.
variants.question: How do you honor backpressure?
variants.expectedPattern: Backoff on 429/Retry-After and pause producers, not hammer the dependency.

variants.title: UI spinner as backpressure
variants.context: The browser fires 30 search keystrokes as 30 HTTP calls with no debounce.
variants.question: Where can pressure start?
variants.expectedPattern: Client-side debounce plus server limits so the origin is not flooded with in-flight searches.
wrongChoices: One HTTP call per keypress with no cap

variants.title: Priority inversion in the buffer
variants.context: Interactive clicks sit behind 10GB of bulk import in one socket buffer.
variants.question: How do you apply pressure fairly?
variants.expectedPattern: Separate queues or admission control so bulk work is slowed first, not user traffic.
wrongChoices: One FIFO buffer for bulk and interactive

variants.title: Disk-backed queue as infinite sink
variants.context: A broker retains everything for 14 days and producers never slow down during a 3-day worker outage.
variants.question: What is still required?
variants.expectedPattern: Retention limits and producer quotas so the log cannot grow without bound.
wrongChoices: Infinite retention as a design goal
Delete consumer groups instead of limiting produce

variants.title: gRPC without flow control awareness
variants.context: A server writes responses as fast as it can while the client is paused, until memory blows.
variants.constraint: HTTP/2 has windowing if you use it.
variants.question: What should the server respect?
variants.expectedPattern: Honor stream flow-control windows; stop sending when the client cannot receive.
wrongChoices: Buffer entire responses in memory always

variants.title: Load shed vs random timeouts
variants.context: Under overload, every request times out after 30s, including cheap ones.
variants.question: What is a better overload policy?
variants.expectedPattern: Shed low-priority or new work quickly so remaining capacity serves high-value requests.
wrongChoices: Let all requests time out together

variants.title: N+1 fan-out without a budget
variants.context: One user request fans out to 400 internal RPCs and the mesh saturates.
variants.constraint: The fan-out is unbounded per request.
variants.question: How do you apply backpressure internally?
variants.expectedPattern: Cap concurrency per request and fail or batch when the budget is exceeded.
wrongChoices: Retry each of the 400 calls three times

variants.title: Mobile sync backlog
variants.context: A device was offline for a week and tries to upload 50,000 events at once.
variants.constraint: The ingest API cannot take that burst from every device.
variants.question: How should the client behave?
variants.expectedPattern: Chunk uploads and respect server 429/backpressure so sync is paced.
wrongChoices: POST the entire week in one body repeatedly

variants.title: Thread pool rejection ignored
variants.context: The executor rejects tasks but the HTTP layer still reads the full body into RAM.
variants.question: When should you apply pressure?
variants.expectedPattern: Refuse work at the earliest gate (accept, auth, or queue) before allocating heavy buffers.
wrongChoices: Catch RejectedExecution and retry inline forever

variants.title: Happy eyeballs on a melting origin
variants.context: Clients open extra connections when slow, which adds more load to a sick origin.
variants.question: What is the backpressure-friendly client policy?
variants.expectedPattern: Retry budgets and hedged requests only when the system is healthy, not under 5xx storms.
wrongChoices: Hedge every slow call during an outage
